nameStory: The 'carpet pelt' name comes from this lichen's habit of spreading across the ground like a living carpet, with its soft, pelt-like texture resembling animal fur. The 'pelt' part refers to how these lichens form leather-like sheets that you can actually peel up from their growing surface, just like a fur pelt!
description: Carpet pelt lichen is a leafy, ground-hugging lichen that forms broad, flat sheets across soil and moss. It has a distinctive two-toned appearance with a gray-green upper surface and a pale underside marked with dark veins. Individual 'leaves' or lobes can spread several inches across, and a single colony might carpet an area the size of a dinner plate or larger.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms large, flat, leafy sheets that lie close to the ground and can be gently peeled up along the edges - feels like thin, damp leather

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Gray-green to blue-green on top when moist, turning more grayish when dry; underside is whitish to cream-colored

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Smooth and slightly glossy upper surface that feels soft and pliable, like wet suede; no powdery coating or bumpy growths

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Always grows on soil, moss, or among low vegetation on the ground - never on tree bark or rocks

idTips.label: Underside Pattern
idTips.description: Pale underside has a distinctive network of raised, dark brown to black veins that branch out like a river system

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual lobes typically 2-4 inches wide, but colonies can spread to cover areas 6-12 inches across or more

habitat: Look for carpet pelt lichen in moist, shaded areas with rich soil in deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England. It particularly favors spots with good air circulation and consistent moisture, like forest floors near streams or in north-facing slopes. You'll often find it growing among mosses and low shrubs in areas that stay damp but don't get waterlogged.

seasonality.spring: Most vibrant after spring rains when the blue-green colors are at their richest and the texture feels most pliable and leather-like. This is an excellent time for identification as colors are most pronounced.
seasonality.summer: May appear more grayish and feel slightly stiffer during dry spells, but summer humidity keeps it relatively supple. Look for it in the coolest, shadiest spots during hot weather.
seasonality.fall: Often looks refreshed by autumn moisture and may be partially hidden under fallen leaves - brush gently to reveal the characteristic smooth surface underneath.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible under light snow cover and actually easier to spot against white backgrounds. The lichen stays flexible even in cold weather, unlike many other ground lichens that become brittle.

funFact: This lichen is essentially a three-way partnership: it contains not just the typical fungus-algae combo, but also nitrogen-fixing bacteria living in special bubble-like structures, making it one of nature's most efficient soil fertilizer factories!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with dog pelt lichen, but carpet pelt has a smoother, more uniform surface while dog pelt has a distinctly 'hairy' or fibrous texture that feels rougher to the touch. Memory trick: carpet pelt feels like smooth carpet, dog pelt feels like dog fur!
contextualKnowledge: Despite having only 3 recorded observations in New England, carpet pelt lichen may be more common than records suggest since it's easily overlooked among other ground vegetation and is often confused with its more common relatives in the pelt lichen family.
compareHints: Carpet pelt lichen differs from its pelt lichen relatives by its consistently smooth upper surface and preference for soil rather than rocks or trees. Unlike the 'hairy' dog pelt lichen or the warty freckled pelt lichen, carpet pelt maintains a clean, uniform appearance. Its lobes also tend to be broader and less divided than the narrow-fingered many-fruited pelt lichen.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the pelt lichens, scaly pelt is the only one in New England with prominent phyllidia scattered across its surface.

Among the many pelt lichens in New England, horizontal pelt lichen is unique for its completely prostrate growth habit - it never curls up at the edges like dog pelt lichen or forms the ruffled, frilly margins of freckled pelt lichen.
Distinguished from dog pelt lichen by having many more fruiting structures along the edges rather than just a few large ones.

Among the many pelt lichens in New England, dog pelt lichen stands out for its preference for growing directly on soil rather than trees, and its particularly well-defined dark veining on a pale underside.
Among the pelt lichens, ruffled freckled pelt stands out for its notably bumpy, textured surface and strongly ruffled edges.
Unlike all other pelt lichens in New England, Eastern Waterfan is the only one that lives in water rather than on soil, rocks, or trees in terrestrial habitats.
Unlike the more common dog pelt lichen which has evenly-spaced, rounded lobes, alternating dog lichen has its distinctive alternating finger-like projections along the edges.
Among the pelt lichens, freckled pelt is the only one with distinctive dark green cephalodia (freckles), making identification fairly straightforward.
Unlike the common dog pelt lichen which has a smooth surface, peppered pelt is distinguished by its dark spotted pattern.
Among its pelt lichen relatives, sheepish pelt lichen is distinguished by its uniquely woolly surface texture - most other Peltigera species have smooth or slightly wrinkled surfaces.
Unlike the common dog pelt lichen which has a relatively uniform surface with veins on the underside, concentric pelt lichen displays obvious ring patterns on top.
Among the many pelt lichens in New England, field dog lichen stands out for its incredibly soft, velvety surface texture - most other dog lichens feel smoother or more leathery.

Among the many pelt lichen species in New England, membranous pelt lichen stands out for its distinctly thin, papery texture - much more delicate than the thicker, more leathery dog pelt lichen or scaly pelt lichen.
Unlike the smooth-surfaced dog pelt lichen or the powdery-edged freckled pelt lichen, mother-of-many pelt is immediately recognizable by its bumpy, phyllidia-covered surface.

Unlike the more common dog pelt lichen which has rounded, disk-like apothecia along the lobe edges, blacksaddle pelt has distinctive tubular, saddle-shaped reproductive structures on the lichen surface.

Compared to its Peltigera relatives, tree pelt lichen has a distinctly more velvety surface texture and tends to be more brownish in color than the grayer dog pelt lichen or the more distinctly veined fan pelt lichen.
Among its pelt lichen relatives, fan pelt lichen stands out with its smooth upper surface and distinctive raised black veins underneath.

Among pelt lichens, the pale-bellied pelt is distinguished by its consistently pale underside, whereas dog pelt lichen has a darker, often brownish underside with prominent veins, and freckled pelt lichen has distinctive dark spots on its upper surface.
